title: Ugh it's not your RACI chart
author: Peters, Leah Celeste
summary: The most expensive decisions are the ones everyone thinks got made. I have lived this as an operator and listened to the recap as a coach...a lot: A team meets. Probably for at least 60-90 minutes. They talk it through, land somewhere, and leave the room feeling good. People scribbled in their notebooks, the AI sent the notes, the google doc running agenda was updated. Then...nothing moves. Three weeks later someone asks about it (or something breaks) and everyone gets four different answers about who owns it, when it's due, and whether it was ever actually decided. No one was trying to undermine the decision or limit action, but the whole thing was an exercise in making a decision rather than taking responsibility for it. I have coached, observed, and worked alongside leaders across sectors and every level of leadership, and the gap between making a decision and executing one is one of the most consistent points of failure. It is also, it turns out, one of the most studied, which surprised (depressed?) me when I went looking. Peter Drucker named the process for actually taking responsibility for a decision in 1967. In The Effective Executive, he wrote that a decision has not been made until people know: the name of the person accountable for carrying it out; the deadline; the names of the people who will be affected by the decision and therefore have to know about, understand, and approve it, or at least not be strongly opposed to it; and the names of the people who have to be informed of the decision, even if they are not directly affected by it. That's the whole thing. It's dated, sure, and it holds up completely. I have a screenshot of my highlighted Kindle page saved, and I text it to people at least monthly (and twice this week alone). Here's what I've observed organizations do: they build elaborate RACI spreadsheets and MOCHA documents. They spend tens of thousands of dollars (and sometimes a lot more) training teams on decision-rights frameworks like Bain's RAPID. And the output of that sizeable resource investment is a) everyone is a little pissed off at each other but hopeful this will fix it, and b) there is a spreadsheet with 500 lines that lives in a folder and never sees the light of day. Despite this very pretty artifact (they are almost always beautifully color coded), decisions still stall or bottleneck or never get made at all or all get made by the same executive that was always doing it. The consulting world has a whole genre of statistics about how most strategies die in execution rather than design, and I'll spare you the parade of suspiciously round numbers. But also - duh. Anyone who has ever worked in an organization or institution can attest to the experience of smiling at a strategy deck and then wondering what the heck happened 6 months later. When role clarity is missing, people burn their energy negotiating uncertainty, managing conflict, and protecting their own job security, none of which is the work. A 2025 study in Human Resource Management followed this into well-being, showing that leaders and coworkers jointly shape role clarity, and that it matters most when everything around the team is changing. And role clarity is one of the documented antecedents of psychological safety itself. Clarity, in other words, is foundational to psychological safety, not something achieved once safety is built. Run the checklist against your named decision-maker If you are struggling to see forward movement, timely decisions, or clean execution, attempt Drucker's list with the decision-maker. (I made a Decision Execution Worksheet if it's helpful! Check it out here, and make a copy: Decision Execution Worksheet ). Can that person name who's accountable? Set the deadline? Identify and reach the people affected, the ones who have to understand it and not actively block it? Inform everyone who needs informing? If the person you've named as the decision-maker does not have the access, information, resources, or authority to do the steps that follow, then they are not, in fact, the decision-maker. Something else holds the real authority, and that is almost certainly where things are stalling. The checklist won't necessarily tell you WHY, but will start to point to WHERE. The gap it exposes typically comes from a few different places (or a combo of them): It's you! The named decision-maker is the bottleneck. Avoidance, capacity, or an unwillingness to do the uncomfortable steps Drucker names. This is the simplest one to address. Note: not easy, simple and hard. It's another authority. Someone else holds the resources, the access, or the veto, whether or not anyone wrote that down. This one is tricky, because it likely traipses into some shadow org chart stuff no one wants to talk about. It's a structural gap. Nobody holds what's needed to execute, because the system was never designed to account for it. This one is also tricky, because it likely requires some parallel work on role and responsibility clarity. AND - more often than not - there's a reason this work hasn't landed anywhere yet. The discomfort IS data I have sat with leadership teams at the highest levels and watched them get deeply uncomfortable the moment they have to actually execute these steps. Naming who is accountable. Committing to a real deadline. Saying out loud the names of the people this will affect and who therefore have a right to know. I have felt that flinch myself, sitting on a team, not wanting to be the one to put a name and a date on the record. That discomfort has a name in the research (see footnote #2). Uncertainty and job insecurity push people toward defensive decision-making, choices made to protect yourself rather than to serve the work, and psychological safety is what reduces it. So when you (or your leadership) team flinches at naming a single accountable person and a date, you are watching self-protection operate in real time. The flinch is telling you how safe it actually is to own a decision in your organization, which is frequently not as safe as your values poster proports. A note on the frameworks I want to be fair to the frameworks, because neither RACI nor RAPID nor MOCHA is a problem in and of itself. Role clarity and decision-rights are really important to organizational and institutional functioning. (I like Molly Graham 's Captains framework for ownership, but I'm a Molly G superfan). Your org / team does need clarity on who does and decides what. The degree of complexity you need and the approach that will work best is highly context dependent. BUT I see a lot of organizations think that the spreadsheet or the acronym is going to fix their decision problems, and it usually doesn't. Hence the title: [insert eye roll] "ugh it's not your RACI chart". This is a Universal Design strategy Obviously I have a lot of opinions about UDL to retain and promote neurodiverse talent (see: my article in Chief Learning Officer ), but I didn't expect a super clear throughline when I initially started writing this. However, everything above is about ambiguity that hides where authority actually lives, the implicit stuff nobody wrote down. And the people in your organization who notice that implicit stuff first, and ask for it to be made explicit, are very often your neurodivergent employees. They are also the people who get punished - implicitly and explicitly - for asking. UNICEF's 2025 manager's guide on neurodivergent talent includes an employee describing exactly this: they ask for clarification so they can do the job accurately, managers read the questions as a challenge to their authority, and colleagues advise them to keep their head down to avoid a negative reaction. If you triangulate that against Drucker's outline for actually taking responsibility for a decision, it means the person asking "who is actually accountable here, what is the real deadline, who has to sign off" is running this 70-year-old checklist out loud...but the organization is likely to characterize it as insubordination. Universal Design for Learning rests on the following principle: design for the margin, and the whole population benefits. The curb cut got built for wheelchairs, and now everyone with a stroller, a suitcase, or a bad knee uses it. A 2025 paper in Frontiers in Psychology makes the workplace version of that argument, calling for universal design that makes work accessible by default, through practices like circulating information ahead of time and stating expectations explicitly, so support doesn't depend on someone first disclosing their neurotype. Making decision rights explicit + mapping execution ownership, deadlines, impact, and communication needs clearly is a kind of curb cut. The evidence that predictability and clear expectations disproportionately help neurodivergent employees is deep and consistent. Autistic employees in particular tend to do their strongest work when expectations, deadlines, and communication are explicit, and to struggle most with vague expectations like meetings without agendas and unwritten social rules. One practitioner framing I keep coming back to is Brene Brown's "clear is kind, unclear is unkind". SAP's Autism at Work program had teams build structured communication charters, agreeing how and when they would share information, and it improved collaboration for everyone on the team, not only the neurodivergent members. In my experience (and well-documented in the research on UDL), when you build a structure to support those who need it most, it turns out everyone was drowning in the ambiguity, too (even if it looked a little different), and the whole team is better for it. The "curb cut" of clear decision rights and expectations for execution have the additional benefit helping to break the neurodivergent glass ceiling. Neurodivergent leaders, especially women and nonbinary people, often mask or hide their identities at senior levels to avoid stigma, which keeps them invisible but also prevents the norms from changing. The baseline underneath that ceiling is brutal. By estimates cited in the neurodiversity research, somewhere around 85 to 90% of neurodivergent adults are unemployed or underemployed, against an estimated 15 to 20% of the population being neurodivergent (see Footnote 6). High-context, implicit decision cultures, the kind where you are supposed to just know who really decides, are the environments that create two significant barriers: masking has the highest cost and the people who need things named / explicit get filtered out long before they reach the rooms where decisions happen. Running Drucker's checklist does more than unstick stalled decisions; when made a habit, it can unlock potential across the talent pool. To be clear, a five line checklist does not deliver neurodivergent inclusion. BUT clarity is an important component of building inclusive workplaces. Psychological safety, similarly, is not the type of thing you crank to the maximum with abandon to produce universally good outcomes. I realize we often talk about it like that, but the research does not support it. A 2025 study in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes found that high psychological safety can actually drag on routine performance unless it is paired with collective accountability. In other words, it emphasizes the importance of the accountability aspects of Drucker's checklist for taking responsibility for a decision. Safety lets people name the hard thing or ask for clarity and what they need; accountability makes sure appropriate action is taken. You need both, or you end up with a comfortable team that ships nothing. But what about my RACI? Sometimes role clarity doesn't exist at all. No assigned decision rights, no shared sense of who owns what, no role clarity. If that's you / your team, by all means do that damn work. It's worth it, and the research backs the payoff: clarity in decision-making roughly doubles the odds of actually improving how work gets done. That is not the usual case, though. Usually the RACI (or whatever framework thing) got built, finalized, and signed off, and then it went decorative. It is hanging out, color-coded, looking cute and authoritative while decisions die in the hallway or the Slack channel or the Teams meeting. When execution stalls, resist the urge to rebuild the chart or change the color coding. Instead: run the checklist. Find the gap. Name whether it's the decision-maker, someone else, the design, or all three. And - just maybe - notice who in your organization has been telling you about that gap all along, probably by asking the questions everyone else learned to stop asking. :) It's almost never your RACI chart. Promise! If you use the Decision Execution Worksheet - let me know! What worked? What sucked? How do we make it better?
